dimensions.axis: What the binding constraint on decarbonization is
poles: Firm, dispatchable clean power is physically necessary, so a grid without nuclear is a grid that keeps burning gas
Wind, solar, storage & transmission can do the whole job, so nuclear is an expensive detour that slows the build-out

dimensions.axis: Whether nuclear’s cost problem is fixable
poles: Overruns are an artifact of one-off designs, stop-start programs & regulatory churn; serial build, SMRs or state procurement fix them
Cost escalation is structural to the technology’s complexity & safety demands; every promised learning curve has failed for fifty years

dimensions.axis: How to weigh catastrophic-but-rare risk against chronic harm
poles: Per terawatt-hour deaths & emissions are the right metric, and by it nuclear is among the safest sources ever built
Low-probability, high-consequence, irreversible events & permanent land loss are categorically different and cannot be averaged away

dimensions.axis: Who should own & pay for it
poles: A strategic public good: state ownership, loan guarantees, regulated rate base or direct subsidy are legitimate and necessary
If it cannot clear a competitive market or unsubsidized auction, ratepayers & taxpayers should not be made to carry it

dimensions.axis: Whether waste & proliferation are solved problems
poles: Deep geological disposal is technically demonstrated and safeguards work; the remaining obstacle is politics, not physics
No country has yet operated a permanent repository at scale, and fuel-cycle expansion spreads enrichment & plutonium capability
National climate & energy-security need should override local veto; permitting delay is itself a harm
Host communities, downwinders, Indigenous nations & uranium-mining regions hold a real veto over what is imposed on their land
Domestic nuclear is the way out of dependence on volatile fuel imports & hostile suppliers
Enrichment, fuel fabrication & reactor exports are dominated by Russia & China, so building nuclear trades one dependence for another

dimensions.axis: Whether the unit of judgment is the technology or the project
poles: Nuclear can be judged as a technology class, and a general verdict should drive policy
Only this reactor, in this market, under this regulator, on this schedule can be judged; first-of-a-kind and life extension are different objects

affected: Electricity ratepayers and taxpayers in countries deciding whether to build, extend or close reactors
Communities hosting reactors, tailings and proposed waste repositories, including downwinders and Indigenous nations on mining and disposal land
Nuclear and fossil plant workforces, building trades, and the towns whose tax base is a single plant
Energy-intensive industry and data center operators seeking firm, low-carbon supply
Populations exposed to fossil air pollution and climate damage where nuclear is or is not displacing coal and gas
Utility regulators, grid operators and system planners who must set reserve margins decades ahead
Uranium miners, enrichment and fuel-cycle workers, and the states that host that supply chain
Future generations who inherit both the waste and the emissions trajectory
Non-nuclear-weapons states whose civil programs are read through a proliferation lens
Low-income countries seeking non-intermittent low-carbon power and the finance to build it

frame_rejection.note: The harvest supports one rejection of the up-or-down frame: agencies and practitioners who insist the unit of judgment is the project and the attribute, not the fuel. The US Energy Information Administration states that direct comparisons of levelized cost across technologies are misleading, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has written a technology-inclusive licensing framework, Germany’s BASE refuses to say SMRs are safer in principle, the Hinkley Point C technical director calls his own plant a first-of-a-kind in a country that had not built for three decades, and California Public Utilities Commission staff propose buying attributes rather than named technologies. The other rejections named in the frame question remain unrepresented: the gap search returned one political ecologist, David Schwartzman, who addresses nuclear directly but answers the question rather than refusing it, and no institutional degrowth, demand-side or energy-democracy claimant appears anywhere in the harvest or the gap return in its own published words.

camps.name: Build new reactors as climate infrastructure
camps.wants: Governments should run programmatic newbuild so that firm, zero-carbon generation grows alongside wind and solar rather than leaving gas to fill the gap.
camps.distinguishing: Affirms that there is no credible path to deep decarbonization without a substantial and growing role for nuclear, which the renewables-instead camp denies.
camps.rank_reason: The most widely held position in the harvest, carried by industry bodies, the IEA, climate scientists, several EU governments, the largest Chinese vendor, building-trades unions and converted environmentalists across every source class.

adherents.name: International Energy Agency
adherents.quote: It does so by exploring in depth nuclear power’s potential role as a source of low emissions electricity that is available on demand to complement the leading role of renewables such as wind and solar in the transition to electricity systems with net zero emissions.

adherents.quote: While it may be theoretically possible to stabilize the climate without nuclear power, in the real world there is no credible path to climate stabilization that does not include a substantial role for nuclear power

adherents.name: George Monbiot
adherents.quote: As a result of the disaster at Fukushima, I am no longer nuclear-neutral. I now support the technology.

adherents.name: Fatih Birol
adherents.quote: Without the support of nuclear power, we have no chance to reach our climate targets on time

adherents.name: China National Nuclear Corporation
adherents.quote: As China’s independently developed third-generation nuclear technology, the Hualong One sets a benchmark with a 68.7-month construction period for its first unit, making it the only third-generation nuclear project delivered on schedule in the world.

adherents.name: North America’s Building Trades Unions
adherents.quote: Vogtle 3 & 4 is currently the largest jobs-producing construction project in the state of Georgia, with more than 9,000 workers currently on site, and more than 800 permanent jobs available once the units begin operating.

adherents.name: 46 environmental organizations from the European Union
adherents.quote: calling to increase share of nuclear power as the most effective way of reducing EU’s reliance on fossil fuels... condemned multi-facetted misrepresentation and rigged information about nuclear, with opinion driven by fear

adherents.name: Tom Greatrex
adherents.quote: The more nuclear stations we build the quicker and cheaper it will become, so instead of building one plant at a time with long gaps in between projects, a programmatic approach, as outlined in the government’s Nuclear Roadmap, is vital to ensure we build expertise, maintain workforce capability and increase efficiency.

adherents.name: W. Gyude Moore
adherents.org: former Liberia Minister for Public Works
adherents.quote: accused high-income countries like Germany and Australia of hypocrisy and pulling up the ladder behind them, as they have built their strong economy over decades of cheap fossil or nuclear power, and now are effectively preventing African countries from using the only low-carbon and non-intermittent alternative, the nuclear power

camps.variation: Instrument and finance differ inside the camp: a state-programmatic wing (Great British Nuclear, EDF, the UK Nuclear Industry Association) wanting fleets of identical units; a US regulated-utility wing relying on federal loan guarantees and rate-base recovery at Vogtle; a state-vendor wing (CNNC) resting the case on serial Hualong One delivery on schedule; a building-trades wing (North America’s Building Trades Unions at Vogtle) arguing from union construction jobs and a permanent operating workforce; a development wing (Moore) arguing rich countries are denying poorer ones the option; and a supply-chain sovereignty wing (US Department of Energy, Bruegel, Nick Timothy) that would build only on non-Russian, non-Chinese fuel and vendors.

camps.name: Replace nuclear with renewables, storage and efficiency
camps.wants: Capital and time should go to wind, solar, storage, transmission and efficiency, and existing reactors should be retired alongside fossil plants.
camps.distinguishing: Affirms that renewables plus storage deliver more carbon reduction per dollar and per year than any nuclear build, which the expand-newbuild camp denies.
camps.rank_reason: The second large bloc, with institutional weight in Greenpeace, IEEFA, the European Environmental Bureau and NIRS, and academic weight in Lovins, Ramana, Jacobson and Schwartzman.

adherents.name: Greenpeace International
adherents.quote: Nuclear energy has no place in a safe, clean, sustainable future.

adherents.name: Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis
adherents.quote: Small modular reactors still look to be too expensive, too slow to build, and too risky to play a significant role in transitioning from fossil fuels in the coming 10-15 years.

adherents.name: Amory Lovins
adherents.org: Precourt Institute for Energy, Stanford University / RMI
adherents.quote: In over 24,000 actual market projects, new unsubsidized renewables make electricity 5–13 times cheaper than nuclear newbuild according to BNEF; merchant bank Lazard analysis finds 3–8 times.

adherents.name: M.V. Ramana
adherents.quote: The path to a world that is secure and ecologically sustainable leads away from nuclear power and small modular reactors.

adherents.name: European Environmental Bureau
adherents.quote: The existing nuclear fleet can be phased out alongside fossil fuels as EU countries transition to a drastically more efficient energy system

adherents.name: Mark Jacobson
adherents.org: Stanford University Atmosphere and Energy Programme
adherents.quote: Every dollar spent on nuclear results in one-fifth the energy one would gain with wind or solar [at the same cost], and nuclear energy takes five to 17 years longer before it becomes available.

adherents.name: Robert Habeck
adherents.org: Germany’s economy and climate action ministry
adherents.quote: We see today that our power supply is secure, that power price dropped also after the nuclear phase-out and that CO2 emissions are going down as well

adherents.name: David Schwartzman
adherents.quote: I submit that the only nuclear power we need is found in the Sun’s core, its fusion reactor, supplying abundant energy to Earth. Building more nuclear fission reactors and the huge investment into on-site nuclear fusion are unwelcome diversions from accelerating the creation of global wind/solar energy supplies.

adherents.name: Georgia WAND
adherents.org: Georgia WAND (Women’s Action for New Directions)
adherents.quote: The truth is, nuclear energy generates dangerous waste, is expensive to produce and poses significant safety and security risks.

camps.variation: Some want operating reactors closed now (Greenpeace, the European Environmental Bureau, Habeck) while others concentrate on stopping newbuild and let the installed fleet run out its licences (IEEFA, Schlissel, Wamsted). A ratepayer-protection wing (Georgia WAND, Patty Durand, the Nuclear Information and Resource Service) argues from bills, disconnections and the FirstEnergy bribery case rather than from climate arithmetic. A political-ecology wing (Schwartzman) argues in labor terms, that a Green New Deal gives energy workers more work decommissioning aged reactors and building renewables than building new ones.

camps.name: Run the existing reactors longer, build no new ones
camps.wants: Operating and recently closed plants should be kept online, relicensed or restarted because they are the cheapest firm low-carbon power available, while new construction is left alone until it can be built without public risk.
camps.distinguishing: Affirms that the reactor already built is the cheapest and fastest firm low-carbon power on offer and should be relicensed, restarted and contracted before anything new is begun, which the renewables-instead camp denies and which the expand-newbuild camp treats as insufficient.
camps.rank_reason: The hybrid that the cost evidence points to most directly, held by the Union of Concerned Scientists, EU officials, economists, and now by the utilities, buyers and trades behind the Three Mile Island restart.

adherents.name: Union of Concerned Scientists
adherents.quote: Nuclear power is the single largest source of low-carbon electricity in the United States.

adherents.name: Joseph Lassiter
adherents.quote: The primary source of nuclear power going forward will be the current nuclear fleet of old plants

adherents.name: Joe Dominguez
adherents.quote: Powering industries critical to our nation’s global economic and technological competitiveness, including data centers, requires an abundance of energy that is carbon-free and reliable every hour of every day, and nuclear plants are the only energy sources that can consistently deliver on that promise.

adherents.name: Bobby Hollis
adherents.quote: This agreement is a major milestone in Microsoft’s efforts to help decarbonize the grid in support of our commitment to become carbon negative. Microsoft continues to collaborate with energy providers to develop carbon-free energy sources to help meet the grids’ capacity and reliability needs.

adherents.name: Rob Bair
adherents.org: Pennsylvania State Building and Construction Trades Council
adherents.quote: The CCEC will support thousands of family-sustaining jobs for decades to come. It will help make Pennsylvania a leader in attracting and retaining the types of reliable, clean energy jobs that will define the future.

adherents.name: Thierry Breton
adherents.org: European Commissioner for the Internal Market
adherents.quote: described shutting down of operational nuclear power plants as depriving Europe of low-carbon energy capacity

adherents.name: Veronika Grimm
adherents.org: German national council of economic experts
adherents.quote: power prices “of course” would be lower if nuclear plants were kept running

adherents.quote: Small modular reactors will generate more expensive electricity than large reactors (which themselves are not economical to build at present). Despite all the hype about the promise of SMRs circulating in the media, they cannot overcome the fundamental principle of economies of scale.

camps.variation: The grounds differ: cost (life extension at 32 USD/MWh is the cheapest dispatchable option), price effects on consumers (Grimm), grid capacity in Europe (Breton), and a risk argument (Lyman) that the operating fleet’s hazards are known while new designs are experimental. A restart-and-offtake wing has formed around the Crane Clean Energy Center, where Constellation, Microsoft and the Pennsylvania building trades argue the fastest firm carbon-free capacity is an existing reactor brought back under a long-term corporate contract; that wing differs in instrument, private offtake rather than public payment, not in aim. They also split on whether it is acceptable to subsidize unprofitable plants to keep them open.

camps.name: Mass-produce small modular reactors
camps.wants: Reactors should be shrunk and factory-built in series so that financing risk, construction time and site-specific cost escalation come down together.
camps.distinguishing: Affirms that serial production of small units is the route to affordable nuclear, which the run-existing-longer camp and the project-by-project camp deny.
camps.rank_reason: A well-funded and heavily covered program with vendor, trade-body and federal backers, but its flagship project was cancelled and no unit is operating in the sources here.

adherents.name: NuScale Power
adherents.quote: NuScale remains the only SMR technology company to have received approval from the NRC for its SMR technology design; today’s announcement marks NuScale’s second design approved by the United States’ nuclear regulator.

adherents.name: Craig Piercy
adherents.quote: Setbacks are to be expected when it comes to pioneering technology like small modular reactors. Advanced nuclear is still coming.

adherents.name: Nuclear Energy Institute
adherents.quote: Innovation — particularly in new technologies — is defined by fits and starts. And innovation in next-generation nuclear is no different.

adherents.name: Bret Kugelmass
adherents.quote: thousands of SMRs could be built in parallel, “thus reducing costs associated with long borrowing times for prolonged construction schedules and reducing risk premiums currently linked to large projects”

adherents.name: Jon Ball
adherents.quote: Ball agreed, saying the modular elements of SMRs would also help reduce costs associated with extended construction times.

adherents.name: Simon Irish
adherents.quote: Terrestrial Energy is deeply disappointed in the poor quality of this article and its numerous and significant factual errors... Such a statement ignores well-established fact in the field: No reactor uses or proposes using pyrophoric fuels.

adherents.name: Christophe Xerri
adherents.org: IAEA Division of Nuclear Fuel Cycle and Waste Technology
adherents.quote: Since this type of small modular reactor will be using the same fuel as conventional, large nuclear power plants, its spent fuel can be managed in the same way as that of large reactors.

camps.variation: One wing rests the case on factory learning and parallel construction (Kugelmass, Ball, and Weinberg’s 1952 power-package argument), another on a siting niche too small for gigawatt plants (Mohre, rural cooperatives). A waste-rebuttal wing (NuScale, Terrestrial Energy, and the IAEA’s fuel-cycle division) contests the Krall, Macfarlane and Ewing result on inputs and on the claim that SMR spent fuel needs new disposal routes. NuScale itself shifted after the Idaho cancellation from a single anchor customer to uprated 77 MWe modules and export customers.

camps.name: Judge each project on its measured attributes
camps.wants: Decisions should be made on what a specific plant, in a specific market, under a specific regulator, delivers on cost, firmness and safety, not on a verdict about the fuel.
camps.distinguishing: Denies that a general verdict on nuclear as a technology class can be drawn from cross-technology cost or safety comparisons, which the expand-newbuild, renewables-instead and smr-serial camps all assume.
camps.rank_reason: Held mainly by regulators, statistical agencies and procurement authorities rather than campaigners, so it is quietly authoritative but rarely argued as a public position.

adherents.name: U.S. Energy Information Administration
adherents.quote: Direct comparisons of LCOE or LCOS across technologies are misleading as a method to assess the economic competitiveness

adherents.name: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission
adherents.quote: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is amending its regulations by adding a risk-informed, performance-based, and technology-inclusive regulatory framework for commercial nuclear plants in response to the Nuclear Energy Innovation and Modernization Act (NEIMA).

adherents.name: California Public Utilities Commission Staff
adherents.quote: PU Code § 454.52(c) states that the CPUC “may order the procurement of resources with specific attributes by load-serving entities as a result of the integrated resource planning process and shall enforce any resource procurement requirements on a nondiscriminatory basis.”

adherents.name: German Federal Office for the Safety of Nuclear Waste Management (BASE)
adherents.quote: it is not possible to state, that a higher safety level is achieved by SMR concepts in principle.

adherents.name: HPC technical director
adherents.quote: In effect HPC is a first-of-a-kind plant in a country that has not built a new plant for three decades

camps.variation: Regulators emphasize technology-inclusive licensing and case-specific safety findings (NRC, BASE, STUK, ASNR); statistical agencies emphasize that levelized cost alone cannot rank technologies (EIA); procurement authorities turn the principle into a purchasing rule, buying attributes on a nondiscriminatory basis rather than naming a fuel (CPUC staff’s proposed Clean Energy Standard); practitioners emphasize that first-of-a-kind, nth-of-a-kind and life extension are different objects with different answers (the Hinkley technical director, EDF on its 20-30% gain when repeating an identical unit).

camps.name: Require the consent of host and mining nations
camps.wants: No mining, milling, reactor or repository should proceed on a community’s land without that community’s consent, whatever the national energy accounting says.
camps.distinguishing: Affirms that affected nations and host communities hold a veto over the whole fuel chain, which the expand-newbuild camp denies when it treats permitting delay as itself a harm.
camps.rank_reason: Narrower than the energy-policy camps, but now carried on two continents by Navajo Nation officials and South Australian Native Title bodies, and it holds a legally enforceable veto in at least one jurisdiction.

adherents.name: SCHEER (Scientific Committee on Health, Environmental and Emerging Risks)
adherents.quote: the SCHEER is of the view that dependence on an operational regulatory framework is not in itself sufficient to mitigate these impacts, e.g. in mining and milling where the burden of the impacts are felt outside Europe

camps.variation: One route is jurisdictional and legal, a tribal statute that bars the activity outright; another is the summit’s demand for a halt to the entire chain from exploration to disposal; a third is the South Australian route, where Native Title corporations and weapons-test survivors put their refusal of a proposed repository to a royal commission; a fourth, SCHEER’s, is regulatory, holding that European assessments cannot certify harms that fall on mining communities outside Europe.

crux_placement.crux: Is the cost of a reactor a fact about the technology or about the way it has been bought — and who carries the risk while that stays unsettled?

placement.note: Reads the overruns as contingent on stop-start, one-off procurement rather than on reactors, and treats firm zero-carbon output as a system need whose delivery risk the public may properly underwrite.

Takes the overruns as intrinsic and settles the question on opportunity cost, but its call to retire the existing fleet, already the cheapest firm low-carbon option, rests on a judgment about catastrophic risk rather than on cost.

Accepts that firm zero-carbon output is worth having and declines to resolve the buildability forecast at all: buy only the reactors whose cost is already known, and wait for someone else to demonstrate the rest.
Locates the cost problem entirely in the build method and bets that factory volume, not physics, is the binding constraint; it stands or falls on whether 40 to 70 units ever get ordered.

Denies that the fork is well-formed at class level, holding that cost, firmness and safety vary more within nuclear than between nuclear and its rivals, so the only answerable question is about a named project.
Sits on the other branch entirely: the dispute is over who holds authority to decide, and no improvement in cost, schedule or safety statistics touches the claim that a host nation may refuse.
